prompt.brief: Design a model registry that immutably stores artifacts and metadata, tracks lineage and model cards, manages lifecycle stages, and gates production promotion with approvals and policy checks.
successSignals: Make an immutable artifact digest plus dataset, code, feature, evaluation, owner, and approval metadata the version authority.
Separate metadata queries from large artifact storage and make promotion a conditional lifecycle transition.
Integrate CI/CD and serving systems through signed manifests, policy gates, webhooks, and idempotent callbacks.
Explain artifact retention, lineage, access controls, rollback, deletion, registry outage, and audit evidence.

functional: Register artifacts, metadata, model cards, evaluation results, dependencies, and immutable versions.
Move versions through draft, validated, staging, canary, production, archived, and rejected lifecycle stages.
Support approvals, policy checks, deployment webhooks, artifact downloads, rollback, deprecation, and audit export.
nonFunctional: Support 100,000 model versions with metadata lookups below 200 ms p95 and immutable artifact downloads through signed URLs.
Partition metadata by tenant, project, model name, and version while isolating high-volume CI/CD integrations.
Make registration, approval, promotion, webhook delivery, and artifact garbage collection idempotent.
Serve the last approved production manifest when new registry writes or evaluation systems are unavailable.
scaleAssumptions: Track 100,000 versions, 10,000 active models, and CI/CD events from hundreds of repositories.
Partition by tenant, project, model, and lifecycle stage; isolate large artifact transfers from metadata reads.
Retain signed manifests, lineage, approvals, model cards, audit logs, and artifact retention decisions.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Model registry commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Model registry writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Model registry version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Model registry by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Model registry work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Model registry projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Model registry projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Model registry records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Model registry latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
